sec.title: Background
sec.p: Preventive periodontal care is essential for older people in the community to reduce the risk of tooth loss, systemic diseases, and decreased quality of life. Despite its importance, older people in assisted living, home‐based care (HBC), daycare, and other community settings face barriers to effective preventive periodontal care, including mobility, cognitive, and caregiver knowledge issues. Although these challenges are being recognized more and more, the evidence on barriers and solutions for delivering consistent preventive periodontal care remains scattered across different study designs and care contexts.

sec.title: Aim and Objective
sec.p: The aim of this scoping review is to map the existing literature and systematically identify the key challenges at patient, caregiver, and institutional levels, along with evidence‐based solutions—including behavior change techniques (BCTs), tools, and interventions—for delivering preventive periodontal care to older adults in community and mixed residential settings.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The Joanna Briggs Institute scoping review method, along with the PRISMA‐ScR, was followed to identify the key issues, solutions, and findings related to the implementation of preventive periodontal care in older people in the community. The inclusion criteria were older people aged 60 years or more, interventions, community, or mixed settings, and the languages were restricted to English. The search was conducted for articles from 2010 or later. Two‐phase selection was used, which yielded 32 articles. This was followed by data extraction, including study design, settings, population, interventions, outcomes, issues, solutions, thematic synthesis, etc.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Thirty‐two studies were included (12 cross‐sectional, 8 RCTs/quasi‐RCTs, 6 systematic reviews/protocols, and 6 others). Included studies were conducted mainly in nursing homes (n = 15), with 10 in community and 7 in mixed settings. Key challenges were identified at the resident, caregiver, and institutional/systemic levels. Resident‐level challenges included cognitive and functional limitations, while caregiver‐level barriers included gaps in knowledge and the relatively low priority given to oral care. At the institutional and systemic levels, workload, limited access to professional dental care, and the lack of standardized oral‐care protocols were frequently reported. Solutions included carer education with BCTs, standardized tools (e.g., Oral Health Assessment Tool [OHAT]), visual aids, AI‐supported screening, regular professional outreach brushing, and interprofessional models, showing modest short‐term improvements in plaque index (PI), gingival index (GI), and bleeding on probing (BOP).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Persistent challenges underscore the need for integrated, accessible strategies to enhance preventive care. Future research should prioritize cost‐effectiveness, community‐focused RCTs, and long‐term evaluations to improve oral health outcomes in aging populations.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The global population is currently undergoing a significant demographic shift, whereby the number of people aged 60 years or older is expected to double in the next 30 years, accounting for 22% of the total population by 2050 [1, 2]. This is a major challenge to the existing healthcare infrastructure, especially regarding the issue of oral health, which, unlike other medical fields, has traditionally followed the reactive rather than preventative model [3]. Periodontal disease (PD) and dental caries are now recognized as the most prevalent noncommunicable diseases, surpassing the combined prevalence of mental diseases, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, respiratory diseases, and cancer [1, 3]. Even among relatively healthy individuals, inadequate oral hygiene has been reported. In a study conducted in Bern, Switzerland, a substantial proportion of participants had an Approximal Plaque Index (API) above 50%, despite most participants reporting that they brushed their teeth twice daily [4, 5]. This finding highlights that reported toothbrushing frequency alone may not necessarily reflect adequate plaque control.

Preventive periodontal care refers to a set of strategies and interventions aimed at preventing the onset and progression of gingival and PDs through the control of bacterial plaque biofilm. It comprises daily oral hygiene practices such as toothbrushing, interdental cleaning, tongue cleaning, and the use of adjunctive chemical agents like chlorhexidine mouth rinses. In addition, it includes regular professional periodontal assessments using clinical indicators such as the plaque index (PI), gingival index (GI), bleeding on probing (BOP), and probing pocket depth (PPD), along with supportive professional interventions such as scaling and root surface debridement when indicated.

Preventive periodontal care also involves patient and/or caregiver education regarding the significance of oral hygiene maintenance, behavior change techniques (BCTs) to support daily oral hygiene maintenance, and the establishment of long‐term maintenance protocols to sustain periodontal health.

New evidence is increasingly coming to light regarding the complex relationship between PD and systemic health [6, 7]. Evidence suggests that PDs are associated with several systemic conditions through shared inflammatory pathways and biological mechanisms; however, many of these relationships remain associative rather than definitively causal. Consequently, maintaining periodontal health is increasingly recognized as an important component of healthy aging and comprehensive healthcare.

Click or tap here to enter text. In this scoping review, community settings refer to environments where older adults live independently or semi‐independently in their own homes or with home‐based support services, including home care recipients and community‐dwelling individuals [8–10].

Mixed residential settings comprise a range of formal care environments such as assisted living facilities, nursing homes, and residential senior care facilities, where older adults with varying levels of dependency receive accommodation and daily assistance [2–5]. These include both assisted living and more intensive long‐term care (LTC) homes, where preventive periodontal care is often delivered through caregivers and institutional protocols [7, 11, 12].

As the older adult transitions from independent to care‐dependent, the first functional skill affected is oral hygiene maintenance [4]. Cognitive impairments, as measured by decreased SMMSE scores, are positively correlated with decreased numbers of natural teeth and reduced masticatory ability [4]. This sets off the downward spiral of memory loss, loss of motor control, and apraxia, leading to oral hygiene neglect, which in turn accelerates cognitive impairments and nutritional deficiencies [4, 13]. Oral hygiene is often deprioritized in the community and LTC settings and is often classified as “missed nursing care.” Care providers often view oral hygiene as merely grooming and not an essential infection control measure [4, 14].

Older adults in the community setting, such as home‐based care (HBC) and assisted living, experience unique barriers to oral health care [5, 8]. Studies from Germany indicate that HBC recipients may experience even lower oral health outcomes than their nursing home counterparts due to the lack of professional oversight and dental contracts in HBC settings [9].

Older adults face several barriers to maintaining adequate oral hygiene across different levels of care. At the patient level, high rates of care‐resistant behaviors, such as biting, screaming, and refusal of oral care, have been reported among older adults with dementia, making routine oral hygiene difficult [7]. At the provider level, knowledge gaps among medical practitioners and caregivers, along with cultural beliefs that tooth loss is an inevitable part of aging, may contribute to inadequate oral care [2, 8]. At the institutional level, high staff turnover and the lack of standardized tools and protocols for monitoring routine oral care have also been identified as important gaps [4, 11].

Current periodontal research literature underscores the significance of proper preventive care in the maintenance of periodontal health. Current evidence shows that regular supportive periodontal care and successful control of periodontal inflammation help ensure periodontal stability, while the effectiveness of particular therapy methods can depend on the clinical state and therapy chosen [15]. It has also been found that the effectiveness of adjunctive antimicrobial therapies in the case of periodontal and peri‐implant diseases is not constant [16, 17].

Thus, recent literature has highlighted the importance of individualized supportive periodontal care, evidence‐based maintenance strategies, and preventive interventions for preserving periodontal health over time. Nevertheless, implementing these preventive approaches among older adults in community and residential care settings remains challenging because of patient‐, caregiver‐, institutional‐, and system‐level barriers. It is especially significant in the case of elderly people whose ability to practice regular oral hygiene, use the services of professionals, and maintain preventive care depends on their physical capabilities, degree of dependency, availability of caregivers, and other peculiarities of care settings. Thus, it is important not only to understand the clinical approach to periodontal prevention but also the barriers and strategies for its implementation.

Aim of the study: The aim of this scoping review is to map the existing literature and systematically identify the key challenges at patient, caregiver, and institutional levels, along with evidence‐based solutions—including BCTs, tools, and interventions—for delivering preventive periodontal care to older adults in community and mixed residential settings.

sec.title: 2. Materials and Methods
sec.p: This study is a scoping review designed to compile and chart the available research evidence, outlining the scope, features, and extent of studies on the topic, and was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines [18]. This review also aligns with PRISMA‐ScR standards “Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews” [18].

The review is guided by this research question framed in the PCC structure: “What are the primary patient, provider, and institutional challenges in delivering preventive periodontal care to older adults in community and residential settings, and what evidence‐based solutions exist to overcome these barriers?”
The review protocol was retrospectively registered publicly on the Open Science Framework (OSF) on March 12, 2026, following completion of the database searches conducted on January 5, 2026.
It is accessible via https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/Q7H4C (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/Q7H4C).
Initial database searches in PubMed, Scopus, EBSCO, and protocol registries confirmed no prior or ongoing reviews addressing this specific question.

sec.title: 2.1. Search Strategy
sec.p: Electronic searches were conducted on January 5, 2026, in PubMed, Scopus, and the EBSCOhost platform MEDLINE via EBSCO for studies published between January 2010 and January 2026. The restriction to publications from 2010 onwards was applied to capture contemporary models of preventive periodontal care relevant to current community and residential aged care services. Only studies published in English were considered. Search terms: ("preventive periodontal care” OR “oral hygiene” OR “periodontal prevention") AND ("older adults” OR “elderly” OR “geriatric") AND ("community settings” OR “assisted living” OR “home‐based” OR “homebound") AND ("challenges” OR “barriers” OR “solutions” OR “interventions").

A search strategy was developed for each database using relevant keywords and MeSH terms, where applicable. The search strategy was adapted for each database. The complete search strategy for each database is presented in Table 1. The retrieved records were exported into Rayyan (https://www.rayyan.ai/) for duplicate removal and screening.

sec.title: 2.2. Selection Process
sec.p: Two independent reviewers (Ankita Chakraborty and Deepa Kamath G) conducted title/abstract screening was conducted against predefined eligibility criteria using the PCC framework (population, concept, context).

Inclusion criteria:•
Population: older adults aged ≥60 years, including frail, dependent, or cognitively impaired individuals.•
Concept: preventive periodontal care, including oral hygiene interventions (toothbrushing, tongue cleaning, chlorhexidine, etc.), periodontal assessments (e.g., PI, GI, BOP, PPD), and related outcomes.•
Context: community settings (homes with or without home care support, assisted living, and daycare centers) or mixed residential settings that include a substantial community component (assisted living facilities, nursing homes, and residential senior care facilities).•
Study types: systematic reviews, RCTs, cross‐sectional, pilot, qualitative studies, and narrative reviews. Primary quantitative studies (randomized controlled trials, quasi‐experimental studies, cross‐sectional and observational studies), qualitative studies, pilot or feasibility studies, systematic reviews, narrative reviews, and study protocols were eligible for inclusion. Qualitative studies were included to identify barriers and implementation issues. Systematic and narrative reviews were included to map the existing evidence base, while study protocols were included to identify ongoing or planned research. These secondary evidence sources were not used as evidence of intervention effectiveness during data synthesis.•
English‐language articles were published from 2010 to January 2026 addressing challenges and/or solutions.

Exclusion criteria:•
Purely institutional/hospital settings without community elements;•
Nonpreventive (restorative/surgical/drug therapy);•
The nonolder adult population (adults aged <60 years);•
Animal studies, editorials, and abstracts without full data;•
Non‐English publication.

In total, 898 records were determined through database searches. No additional records were identified from other sources. Following the removal of duplicates, 850 unique records underwent title and abstract screening through a dual‐reviewer process. Of these, 556 records were excluded based on the eligibility criteria. The remaining 294 full‐text articles were retrieved and assessed independently by two reviewers for eligibility. Following full‐text assessment, 262 articles were excluded for predefined reasons, resulting in the inclusion of 32 studies in the final scoping review.

Disagreements between reviewers were resolved by discussion and, if unsolved, by a third reviewer (Nina Shenoy). Following full‐text assessment, 32 studies were deemed relevant and included in the final scoping review.

Consistent with PRISMA‐ScR guidance, no formal methodological critical appraisal of included studies was undertaken as the purpose of this review was to comprehensively map the available evidence rather than assess the certainty of evidence. Eligibility assessment and methodological appraisal were therefore treated as distinct processes.

The unit of analysis was the individual publication. Primary studies, secondary reviews, and study protocols were charted separately. Systematic reviews were included to map the breadth of the existing evidence, whereas protocols were included to identify ongoing or planned research. Protocols were not interpreted as evidence of intervention effectiveness.

Records were managed in Rayyan software (https://www.rayyan.ai/), where duplicates were removed prior to screening. The full texts of the remaining 294 reports were retrieved and appraised for eligibility. A PRISMA‐ScR flowchart (Figure 1) details the process, with reasons for exclusions being documented.

sec.title: 3.1. Descriptive Summary of Studies
sec.p: The 32 included articles provided a diverse body of evidence on preventive periodontal care for older adults, with a focus on community and mixed settings. Study designs were varied and included primary studies (cross‐sectional surveys, randomized and quasi‐randomized controlled trials, pilot/feasibility studies, and qualitative studies), secondary evidence (systematic and narrative reviews), and study protocols. These evidence types were considered separately during data synthesis to minimize overlap between primary studies and secondary evidence. Settings predominantly represented nursing homes (n = 15), followed by community settings (n = 10) and mixed community‐residential settings (n = 7). Populations targeted older adults aged ≥60 years (mean ages ranging from 70–85), with sample sizes from small pilots (N = 12–48) to large surveys (N = 527–3426). Many participants were frail or dependent, often with comorbidities like dementia, mobility issues, or polypharmacy. Figure 2 describes the study settings and study design distribution across the 32 articles.

(A) Study designs: cross‐sectional surveys (n = 12, 38%), RCTs/quasi‐RCTs (n = 8, 25%), systematic reviews/protocols (n = 6, 19%), pilot/feasibility studies (n = 4, 13%), qualitative/intervention studies (n = 2, 6%). (B) Study settings: nursing homes (n = 15, 47%), mixed settings (n = 7, 22%), community settings (n = 10, 31%). Community settings include assisted living, home‐based care, and daycare centers.

sec.p: Key periodontal outcomes measured included PI, GI, BOP, PPD, community periodontal index (CPI), mucosal‐plaque score (MPS), tongue coat score, and oral malodor. Effect sizes were generally modest and short‐term, with interventions reducing plaque and gingival indices (e.g., p < 0.05 to p < 0.01), though long‐term sustainability was inconsistent. For instance, short‐term daily interventions (5 days) showed significant reductions in PI and GI (p < 0.01), while longer protocols (3 months to 6 years) improved MPS acceptability from 36% to 70% but left 30% unsatisfactory due to resident factors.

Primary studies informed the synthesis of reported barriers and intervention outcomes, whereas systematic reviews were used to contextualize the findings. Study protocols were mapped as ongoing research and were not interpreted as evidence of intervention effectiveness.
Thematic synthesis revealed two primary domains: challenges and solutions, with subthemes drawn from cross‐study patterns.

sec.title: 3.2. Challenges
sec.p:
Challenges were identified at the resident, caregiver, institutional, and systemic levels, often intersecting to create a “downward spiral” of oral health decline [4]. These barriers were prevalent in the majority of articles, with a focus on dependency and access issues in community‐like settings (e.g., assisted living and HBC).•
Resident‐level barriers: cognitive and functional decline among older adults was one of the most consistently reported barriers across the included primary studies, including dementia‐related resistance, motor skill loss, and low self‐perception of oral health. For instance, Saarela et al. [4] note that cognitive impairments (measured by decreased Standardized Mini‐Mental State Examination, i.e. SMMSE scores) correlated with fewer natural teeth and reduced masticatory ability, leading to a spiral of neglect, nutritional deficiencies, and accelerated decline. Willumsen et al. [13] reported “care‐resistant” behaviors (e.g., biting and screaming) in nearly 97% of dementia patients, making daily care difficult. Dounis et al. [5] highlighted self‐rated poor hygiene and irregular dental visits, with residents not prioritizing impairment until function was affected. In homebound contexts, Gluzman et al. [8] described 33% people experiencing oral pain and 92% people with unmet needs due to functional impairment, considering systemic risks like malnutrition.•
Caregiver‐level barriers: knowledge gaps, lack of confidence, and de‐prioritization of oral care were consistently reported across multiple studies. Saarela et al. [4] explained that caregivers view oral hygiene as “grooming” rather than infection control, leading to “missed nursing care”. Tada et al. [14] identified that cultural misconceptions (e.g., tooth loss as an inevitable part of aging) among medical practitioners result in poor care. De Visschere et al. [11] note that nursing staff often find oral care “unpleasant,” prioritizing other tasks due to limited skills.•
Institutional and systemic barriers: workload, inadequate staffing, lack of standardized protocols, and limited access to professional dental care were recurrent barriers reported across studies conducted in nursing homes, assisted living facilities, and home care settings. De Visschere et al. [11] highlighted that high turnover, insufficient manpower, and no structured protocols lead to unsatisfactory plaque levels even after 5 years. Gluzman et al. [8] pointed to logistical barriers (96% had no access to a dentist since being homebound, mean duration of 3.2 years) and absence of mandates in homebound older adults, unlike nursing homes. Dounis et al. [5] reported structural/financial obstacles (64% find access difficult and no in‐house services).

Overall, the included primary studies suggest that these resident‐, caregiver‐, and institutional‐level barriers may contribute to poor oral hygiene, increased plaque accumulation, and reduced access to preventive periodontal care. Several studies also discussed potential implications for systemic health; however, these associations should be interpreted with caution, as the frequency with which barriers were reported across publications does not necessarily reflect their prevalence among older adults [11, 13].

list-item.p: The “Train‐the‐Trainer” model: this approach, where a professional (e.g., a dental hygienist) trains a “ward oral health organizer,” has proven effective in increasing the consistency of daily care [6]. Manchery et al. [27] show that carer education for short‐term plaque reductions in dementia patients is effective.

Motivation‐based programs: long‐term studies show that combining staff motivation with practical tools can yield significant results. Samson et al. [28] described a program with staff motivation, procedure cards, and equipment, improving MPSs from 36% to 70% acceptable over 6 years. Reisine et al. [20] used motivational interviewing and campaigns for GI reductions (1.15–0.49 at 3 months).

Person‐centered support: programs using person‐centered approaches provided caregivers with specific techniques to manage “care‐resistant” behaviors in residents with dementia, reframing oral care as essential hygiene control rather than a mere grooming task [20].

sec.title: 3.3.2. Standardized Protocols and Tools
sec.p:
Consistency in care is addressed through the implementation of validated assessment tools and innovative technology.•
Standardized assessment: [9].•
Digital and AI innovations: a pilot validation study reported a sensitivity of 93% for detecting gingivitis using an AI‐supported smartphone application. Although promising, further studies are required to establish its clinical effectiveness, feasibility, specificity, acceptability, and cost‐effectiveness before widespread implementation [23].•
Visual guidance: The use of personalized oral health instruction forms (POIFs), which include visual markers and intraoral photos, was associated with greater reductions in plaque accumulation than verbal instructions alone) [24, 28, 30].

sec.title: 3.3.3. Clinical and Outreach Interventions
sec.p:
Bringing professional care directly to community and residential settings circumvents major access barriers.•
Professional Brushing: regular brushing performed by a dental nurse (e.g., every two to 3 weeks) has been shown to improve the nutritional status and quality of life of residents, even when daily nursing staff care is insufficient. Tashiro et al. [29] compared short‐term methods (5 days): toothbrushing reduced PI/GI (p < 0.01), tongue cleaning reduced coat (p < 0.05), and chlorhexidine decreased infections (p < 0.05). Zenthöfer et al. [30] showed that regular professional brushing enhanced QoL and nutrition. Barbe et al. [25] advocated shortened outreach therapy (3 months) for PPD/BOP improvements.•
Mobile and domiciliary services: expanding outreach through mobile dental teams and shortened on‐site therapy cycles can improve clinical markers like pocket depth and BOP in frail populations [14].

sec.title: 3.3.4. Economic and Interdisciplinary Workforce Models
sec.p:
Sustainable solutions require shifting from fragmented care to integrated medical‐dental models.•
Cost‐effectiveness: [2, 7].•
Interprofessional education (IPE): Several studies proposed integrating oral health training into nursing and medical curricula and identifying oral health champions [2] within the workforce; however, these recommendations require further evaluation before routine implementation [2].

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: This scoping review identifies major challenges and feasible solutions for preventive periodontal care among older adults in community settings. The 32 included sources comprised different study designs and settings, with 15 studies conducted in nursing homes, 10 in community settings, and 7 involving mixed settings. Thus, the available evidence was weighted toward nursing home and other long‐term residential care environments, while evidence from independently living and homebound older adults was comparatively limited. The findings should therefore be interpreted according to the setting in which the evidence was generated rather than generalized across all community‐dwelling older adults [11, 28]. Recent periodontal literature also highlights the necessity of having effective periodontal and peri‐implant management via appropriate preventive and supporting procedures. Contemporary research shows that the results of the procedure can differ depending on the condition, the type of treatment used, and the period of follow‐up, emphasizing the necessity of having individual and evidence‐based periodontal care [15–17]. Specifically, supportive periodontal care is critical for sustaining the results of treatment by preventing the recurrence of the disease and having a stable condition of the periodontal and peri‐implant tissues [15, 17]. The mentioned aspects become especially important when it comes to older adults, who can have physical problems, impaired cognition, dependence, absence of caregivers, and a lack of professional dental care. Consequently, while there is evidence of the necessity of proper periodontal care, its provision remains challenging in practice. Evidence from assisted living conditions and home care reveals heightened challenges when frail patients depend on family caregivers or rotating nonspecialist staff for daily oral hygiene. These findings emphasize the critical role of periodontal care in preserving masticatory function, preventing systemic infections, and maintaining nutritional status in population comprising older adults in such community settings [4, 8].

Problems with memory, manual dexterity, mobility, and cooperation pose significant challenge. For many older adults, especially those with dementia or high levels of dependency, everyday tasks like remembering to brush or having the manual dexterity to clean teeth properly become extremely difficult. This might lead to strong resistance, like turning away or becoming agitated while receiving care, which can overwhelm caregivers [7, 12]. Most of these findings were observed in dependent and institutionalized populations, which may not be representative of all community‐dwelling older adults.

Limited access to professional dental care is another major issue, especially among homebound older adults. One study found that 92% of participants had unmet oral health needs, largely because going to a dentist was difficult because of transportation barriers. Another study reported that 96% of homebound older adults had not seen a dentist for an average of 3.2 years [15].

Transportation, financial difficulties, and limited availability of dental services were reported as important reasons for poor access [5, 15]. However, these figures describe the populations studied in those individual studies and should not be interpreted as the prevalence of unmet dental needs among all homebound older adults.

There were also frequent reports of barriers posed by caregivers. Nursing staff and care workers may be less knowledgeable or confident in doing oral care, especially for older adults with dementia or care‐resistant behaviors [9, 30]. Some studies reported that oral hygiene was not given as much importance as other components of daily care. These findings point to how caregiver education and practical training might enhance the provision of daily oral care. Available studies differ in their interventions, populations, and follow‐up periods. Therefore, the available evidence does not establish that one educational approach is superior to the others.

The delivery of oral care can also be affected by institutional factors. Several researchers reported workloads of staff, staff turnover, lack of training, and lack of standardized oral care procedures [9, 29]. Because of these issues, oral hygiene might depend on personal staff practices rather than being part of the standard [9, 25]. Such barriers appear particularly relevant in long‐term residential settings, while home care settings may face additional problems related to access to dental professionals.

Several possible solutions were identified. Education and behavior‐change approaches, including train‐the‐trainer programs and person‐centered strategies, were associated with improvements in oral care practices or short‐term oral health outcomes in some studies [16, 18, 31, 35].

Caregivers can learn the importance of oral care and manage the difficulties associated with dementia through these approaches. Nonetheless, the existing evidence is constrained by variations in the intervention design, sample size, context, and follow‐up duration. To understand whether these benefits can be sustained over the long term, additional research is required.

Regular oral care can be supported by structured assessment tools and visual instructions. The Oral Health Assessment Tool (OHAT) can help non‐dental staff identify oral health problems and when referral may be needed [6]. However, it is a general OHAT and not a substitute for a periodontal examination or diagnosis. Like personalized visual instructions have been beneficial in certain studies [28], their use in other community and residential settings requires further examination.

Digital technologies are an emerging area. An AI‐assisted smartphone app has reported a sensitivity of 93% for detecting gingivitis [27], but this result alone is not enough to establish specificity, efficacy, feasibility, acceptability, and cost‐effectiveness.

Interventions aimed at professionals and outreach efforts might also help with improving access to dental care. While interventions, which included professional brushing of teeth, domiciliary care, mobile clinics, and other types of outreach activities, showed some improvement in the oral or periodontal status of residents [10, 20, 21, 24], it should be noted that due to the differences in setting, design of interventions, and follow‐up period, evidence suggests the possible benefits but cannot confirm any long‐term periodontal and systemic effects of the abovementioned interventions among all older people.

Economic evidence was also limited, as there was no information that can prove the cost advantages of on‐site care in comparison with other approaches [8, 22]. The cost‐effectiveness needs further examination. In general, several useful approaches were identified during the examination of existing literature related to preventive periodontal care, such as oral‐care protocol, caregiver education, regular oral health assessment, proper referral pathway, and outreach services. However, the gathered evidence is not solid enough to make certain measures compulsory, such as professional training and using mobile periodontal clinics [12, 25, 28–30, 34].

sec.title: 4.1. Evidence Limitations
sec.p: The reliability and transferability of the evidence are constrained by the heterogeneity of the included studies. Nursing home residents represented a large proportion of the subjects, whereas independent living or homebound older individuals were not well represented. Many studies were cross‐sectional or had small samples and short follow‐up. Qualitative research provided valuable information about experiences and barriers; however, qualitative data is not an indicator of the prevalence of these issues. Similarly, the number of articles reporting a barrier also do not give an idea of its prevalence. Reviews and protocols gave the background, whereas systematic and narrative reviews provided context; however, neither type provides evidence for effectiveness. Furthermore, including secondary reviews along with primary research increases the chance of overlapping data in the evidence base, thus increasing the risk of some results being considered twice.

Other limitations include the restriction to English‐language publications, which may have introduced language bias, and the 2010 publication date limit, which was intentionally applied to exclude older literature that was considered less relevant to current clinical practice, but this may still have resulted in the omission of some earlier evidence.

Future research should concentrate specifically on independent older adults and those who live at home. The well‐designed longitudinal and controlled study should investigate caregiver education, structured oral care, professional support, and outreach service and specify the type of setting, dependency of the participants, intervention, comparison group, duration of follow‐up, and periodontal outcomes. Health economic research is necessary in order to estimate the cost‐effectiveness of different models of care. Research in various geographic and socioeconomic settings will make the evidence more applicable. Future studies could also include inflammation and other systemic outcomes in order to investigate the systemic effect of periodontal preventive care, but the outcomes should not be assumed but proved.

sec.title: 5. Conclusion
sec.p: This scoping review highlights the persistent multilevel barriers to delivering effective preventive periodontal care for older adults in community and mixed residential settings. Issues such as cognitive and physical decline in residents, low prioritization of oral hygiene, gaps in caregiver knowledge and confidence, heavy workloads with less caregiver staff, and poor access to professional dental support often lead to inadequate plaque control. These problems, in turn, increase the risk of malnutrition and aspiration pneumonia and hence cause a noticeable decline in quality of life.

Several practical solutions appear promising, including tailored training programs for caregivers that incorporate BCTs, simple tools like the OHAT, visual aids with intraoral photographs, AI‐assisted screening apps, regular professional outreach brushing, and stronger collaboration between dental and medical teams. However, most of these interventions only produce modest, short‐term improvements in key periodontal outcomes, namely, PI, GI, and BOP.

Overall, the findings highlight the need to develop integrated preventive strategies that work across both community and residential environments. Policymakers should consider making oral health protocols mandatory in community care systems (similar to what is already required in many nursing homes) with regular staff training, mobile and accessible dental services, and better interprofessional support to address the needs of homebound older adults.

Although this review provides useful insights, limitations still exist, especially the heavy reliance on nursing home data and the lack of long‐term studies focused specifically on community settings, especially in low‐resource contexts. Future research should prioritize cost‐effectiveness evaluations, biomarker assessments, and well‐designed trials in real‐world community and rural settings. Strengthening preventive periodontal care in these ways could make a meaningful difference to both oral and general health in our rapidly aging population.
